cards.front: Recall a key point about Classical Sociologists
cards.back: Durkheim (1858-1917): founding figure of sociology. Key ideas: social facts (external forces that constrain behaviour - laws, norms, religion), collective conscience (shared beliefs and values binding society together), anomie (normlessness when social regulation breaks down). Studied suicide rates to show social factors influence even the most personal act.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Classical Sociologists
cards.back: Marx (1818-1883): society is shaped by class conflict. Key ideas: historical materialism (economy shapes society), alienation (workers are disconnected from their labour under capitalism - they don't own what they produce), false consciousness (workers don't realise they are exploited), revolution (the proletariat will overthrow capitalism creating a classless society).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Classical Sociologists
cards.back: Weber (1864-1920): society cannot be reduced to economics alone. Key ideas: rationalisation (modern society is dominated by efficiency, calculation and bureaucracy - an 'iron cage'), the Protestant Ethic (Calvinist beliefs about predestination encouraged hard work and saving, creating capitalism), verstehen (understanding social action by interpreting the meanings people attach to it).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Classical Sociologists
cards.back: Comparing the classical thinkers: Durkheim focused on social facts and consensus; Marx focused on class conflict and exploitation; Weber focused on meaning and rationalisation. Durkheim and Marx are structural (society shapes individuals); Weber combines structural analysis with understanding individual meanings.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Classical Sociologists
cards.back: Continued relevance: Durkheim's anomie explains modern alienation; Marx's class analysis explains inequality; Weber's rationalisation explains bureaucracy and disenchantment. Each provides a different lens for understanding contemporary society.

cards.front: What should you know about sociology exam tips?
cards.back: When discussing classical sociologists, always: state their key ideas clearly, use specific concepts (not vague generalisations), apply their ideas to modern examples, and evaluate whether their theories still apply to 21st century society.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Durkheim, Marx and Weber are no longer relevant because society has changed so much since their time.
